analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to offer community solar so renters and others without usable roofs can buy into solar power.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 26, 2025 with 12 Democratic cosponsors and referred to two House committees, the bill has had no hearings, marks, or votes since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every electric utility in the country to offer a community solar program, in which customers — including renters and people in apartments who cannot put panels on a roof — subscribe to a share of a nearby solar array and get credits that lower their electric bills. It orders the Department of Energy to run a program to expand access, especially for low- and moderate-income households, provide technical help to state, local, and Tribal governments, and let states that already have comparable programs skip the process. It also lengthens the maximum federal government contract for public utility services to 30 years.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, apartment dwellers, and low- and moderate-income households whose roofs cannot host solar panels would be able to subscribe to a shared community solar array and receive credits that reduce their monthly electric bills, since the bill requires utilities to offer such programs with equitable access for all ratepayers including low-income ones. Community solar developers and the utilities that own or operate the facilities also gain a larger, federally supported market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and households without usable roofs

how_it_helps.text: Every non-tribal electric utility would have to offer a community solar program with 'equitable and demonstrable access' for all ratepayers, including low-income households.
Subscribers could use the value of electricity generated by a shared community solar facility to offset the charges on their own utility bills.

The Energy Department would have to stand up a program within a year aimed at people without regular access to rooftop solar, especially low- and moderate-income individuals, aligned with existing federal low-income programs.

State, local, and Tribal governments would get technical help designing affordable rate structures, and National Laboratories would publish data to help private entities finance and run community solar facilities.
The bill requires a mechanism allowing utilities, non-utilities, and other entities to take ownership stakes in community solar facilities, aimed at preventing market concentration.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities would bear new obligations to design and run community solar programs, with implementation costs likely recovered through rates paid by their customer base. Federal taxpayers bear the cost of expanded Energy Department financing and technical assistance. The 30-year contract provision shifts long-term price risk in federal utility contracts onto government agencies.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement runs through state utility regulators, who get one year to begin and two years to complete consideration of the community solar standard, and states that have already implemented or even just held a proceeding on a comparable standard are exempt — so coverage could be patchy and delay-prone.

The bill directs the Energy Department to expand only its 'existing' grant and loan programs 'to the extent practicable' and provides no dedicated funding, so the federal push relies on resources that may not be there.

How much a subscriber actually saves depends on the credit rate each state regulator sets during implementation; the bill sets the access requirement but not the price of the benefit, and program costs could be spread across a utility's broader ratepayer base.
Extending federal public utility contracts to 30 years locks government agencies into very long-term electricity deals, which could be costly if prices or technology change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but uneven: renters and lower-income households in states that move quickly could see modest bill savings, while coverage elsewhere depends entirely on state regulators choosing to act, and states that have already considered the idea are exempt. The cost is diffuse — program administration and credit design get spread across a utility's ratepayer base and federal financing programs — with no dedicated funding attached. The bill is a reasonable, mid-sized consumer-access measure rather than a sweeping one; its main design weakness is that it mandates a process, not a result, so how much subscribers actually save is left to state-by-state rate design. The 30-year federal contract extension is an unrelated give to utility contractors tucked into a consumer bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since June 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor of Florida introduced the Community Solar Consumer Choice Act of 2025 on June 26, 2025, joined by 11 other House Democrats.
The same day, the House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee; no further action appears in the record.
The bill has 12 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

The bill's core provision amends a 1978 utility law to require each non-tribal electric utility to offer a community solar program that all ratepayers, including low-income ones, can equitably access.
States would have one year to begin and two years to complete consideration of the community solar standard, with states that already acted exempt.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: electric utilities keep the status quo in which renters and roofless households generally cannot access solar savings, and community solar developers gain nothing. The bill's supporters have only a referral to show.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Electric utilities; the bill sits unused

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 26, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears in the record.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 26, 2025; no action on the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; the bill sits in committees controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: Utilities would be required to offer community solar programs whose credits reduce billed revenue, but they gain a mandated role as program operators and permitted facility owners, plus federal public utility contracts stretched to 30 years. Their core interest in billing customers at full rate runs against the bill's purpose, even though the bill makes them the delivery channel.

A federal mandate for utility community solar programs, DOE financing, and published market data would create a nationwide subscriber base and easier financing for companies that build and operate shared solar arrays. Their gain comes with the public's, since both depend on more community solar getting built.

analysis.trajectory: A Democrat-only energy bill referred to two committees run by the House Republican majority, with no hearings or markups on record, follows the path of most legislation at this stage: it is likely to remain in committee and receive no floor vote this Congress. It could advance only if it attracts bipartisan cosponsors and committee leadership chooses to act.
